# 08-fresco — sources

Back-test entry `08-fresco.yaml`: Fresco, the AI scribe for construction superintendents (YC Fall 2024).
Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim from the page named; "Author's choice" marks the
smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent.

Main sources:
- [HN] Launch HN: Fresco (YC F24), 2024-11-21 — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42204939
- [LYC] Launch YC: Fresco, the scribe for construction, 2024-10-23 — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/M73-fresco-the-scribe-for-construction
- [YCP] YC company page — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/fresco (now "AI-powered takeoff and estimating for Division 8 construction")
- [KOE] A contractor's daily-log expectations on Procore's support site — https://support.procore.com/tc/Koester/Site_Map/Koester_Expectations_-_Daily_Logs
- [SWI] Swiftask, Procore daily reports page (vendor) — https://swiftask.ai/ai-integration/procore/intelligent-daily-reports
- [BLS] BLS Occupational Outlook, construction managers — https://www.bls.gov/ooh/management/construction-managers.htm
- [OPU] Launch HN: Opusense (field reports for site inspectors), 2025-05-20 — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44042791

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Construction superintendents on commercial jobs.
   [HN] "Superintendents are the busiest and most expensive people on construction sites."
   [LYC] "That’s the reality for 210k+ construction superintendents (or supervisors, foremen, PMs, etc.) across the USA."
   → `roles[superintendent]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: "on commercial jobs" (the founders ask
   for introductions to commercial general contractors in [LYC]).

2. **What (the job).** Keep the record of the day's work, for liability and disputes.
   [HN] "30-200 photos per day to document site progress (mostly for liability reasons, or in case of a dispute with the
   owner over delays and deliverables)"; photos used to create "daily logs", "structured documents that account for the
   work done on site on any given day". [KOE] the log is "a critical piece of documentation in the arbitration of a
   dispute". → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At the end of the day, after the site walks, in the trailer.
   [HN] "At the end of the day, they'll spend a few hours uploading those photos into OneDrive, or project management
   software like Procore or ACC." [YCP] "We were curious what superintendents were doing for hours in their trailers at
   the end of the day." [LYC] "supes are spending up to 3 hours a day creating documents". → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: daily log`.
   Author's choice: the recall window {5, WORKING_DAYS} and Frequency 4 to 5 working days out of 5 (the posts say "per
   day"; a five-day site week is assumed). Prevalence `p_80_100` ("Nearly all") follows from the same "per day".

4. **Which people (the comparable group).** Superintendents at US general contractors whose jobs run on Procore or ACC.
   [LYC] "210k+ construction superintendents ... across the USA"; "Project management tools like Procore and ACC have
   dramatically increased documentation requirements". [YCP] "driving to Napa, South Bay, and around SF". → `context.segment`,
   `market: US`.

5. **Who pays.** The general contractor, per site.
   [HN] "we charge per site per month, which includes unlimited users on any given construction project".
   → `persona.decision_maker: {role: contractor}`, the BUYER role. Author's choice: the decider is the contractor's
   "operations lead" and the role to test is "The CFO" (a second role, "The project executive", listed); Purchase
   friction's three steps ("A trial on one live job" tested, a Procore check, a security review) and Commitment's step
   "start a paid pilot on one site" are the author's. Public material names no buyer title; [LYC] asks for
   introductions to general contractors by firm, not by role.

6. **Mechanism.** Narrated short videos turned into notes, texted to the crew, pushed to Procore/ACC.
   [HN] "Supers simply take short videos with voiceover, or upload photos, and Fresco does the rest, creating notes with
   transcription, photos, assignees, and due dates. Supers can easily text their crew action items, and receive texts
   back". "We also route this to whatever project management software they're using with a single click."
   [LYC] the narrated example "The beam in the southwest corner of room 134 is corroded and needs replacement by Alex.";
   "Supes who use Fresco complete their notes, on average, 90% faster."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility and Adoption friction items. Relative advantage's two
   benefits are from [HN] ("during their site walks, not after") and [LYC] ("90% faster"); their wording is the author's.

7. **Price.** About $1k per site per month, less with multi-site or multi-month terms.
   [HN] "The typical price is $1k/month, but we offer discounts for multi-month or multi-site commitments."
   → `commercial.price` {800, 1000, month}. Author's choice: the low end of $800 stands for the stated discounts.
   Existing sacrifice: 30 to 60 hours a month per site at an hourly rate of 55 — from [LYC] "up to 3 hours a day" and
   [HN] "a few hours uploading", taken as 1.5 to 3 hours on about twenty working days (author's arithmetic). The rate is
   [BLS] "$55.28 per hour" (median, construction managers, May 2025), the author's stand-in: no superintendent wage is
   in the public material. Ability to pay is derived by code (24% to 61%).

8. **Occasions.** The narrated beam; a school refit report; the uploads and logs at the end of the day.
   [LYC] on a school refit walkthrough: "Normally, creating the final report takes 2+ hours."
   [HN] "few supers have time to do this thoroughly, so these photos aren't very searchable." No named customer quote
   exists in public; the occasions below are scripted from these and from practitioner comments.

## Open
- The verdict was scripted to be plausible and not obviously "build": the problem holds on how often but people
  disagree on whether the log is one of their two worst difficulties; the solution splits on the benefit and on
  talking over videos on site; the price fails (two of eight at the founder's band or above) while the cost it would
  replace is above the price. This is the author's reading of the thread's sceptics, not a measured result.
- No public account names a buyer title at a general contractor; the decider, the tested role "The CFO", the purchase
  steps and the Commitment step are the author's.
- hourly_rate 55 is a proxy (construction managers, not superintendents).
- Existing sacrifice picks use `period: quarter` (the corpus's convention), although the registry's recall period for a
  monthly cost reads "last month"; the values are the monthly figures times three.
- The window {5, WORKING_DAYS} is the author's; the public posts say "per day".

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: Omar, Faith and Trevor all weigh the price against what logs cost them in hours or overtime today, the group name is plain, and none of the four left alone (trial first, per-user pricing, legal-record risk, a second software fee) belongs in that group.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line; every answer is about price, so nothing junk was grouped.

founder.order_why: It runs the way I'd pitch Fresco: the superintendent's day and the end-of-day log, then the problem, then narrated videos turned into notes, then who pays per site and what it costs the contractor, and only then the pilot and the link.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 4 carry the same kicker and the same question, so they read as one context question asked twice. Screen 10 (who decides and pays) is asked again in substance on screens 15-16 (buyer-payer alignment), right after screen 14 has already named the contractor operations lead.
founder.missing: On the cost screen (12) I couldn't give the superintendent's hourly rate. I'd count the 1.5 to 3 hours a day at about $55 an hour, not at a default I can't see. I also wasn't asked whether the price is per site or covers several sites, which matters because I charge per site with unlimited users and discount multi-site or multi-month commitments.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: It goes from what the daily log costs us now, to what Fresco is worth, to who signs, to the Procore check, to a pilot, which is how I'd actually work through a buy, though the numbering skips from 2 of 6 to 4 of 6 around the follow-up.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: How many active job sites we run, since a per-site price only means something against our site count, and what we already pay for daily logs (Procore's own log or another add-on), and whether per-site pricing covers unlimited users.

screens.why4: It is a free-text box with a clear limit of two roles and four words each, 'Nobody' is allowed as an answer, and the 'I'm not sure' escape fits a founder who hasn't mapped the approval chain.
screens.why5: My decider is carried over as I set it, and the box took my two roles, 'The CFO; The project executive', in my words and my order.
screens.why7: This matches the card's founder role_list: at most two roles besides the decider, up to four words each, 'Nobody' allowed, and 'I'm not sure' as the founder's escape, so both of my typed roles can go forward to Check.

screens.why1: Right after I named who has to agree besides the operations lead, it makes sense to show me the whole cast back and let me check it before Keel builds the belief.
screens.why2: Superintendent, operations lead, CFO and project executive are all words I use every day, and the tags (has the problem, decides to buy, has to agree) are plain; only the title being repeated as the intro's first words reads a little clumsily.
screens.why3: Who runs into the daily-log pain, who signs a per-site tool and who has to bless a $1k-a-month line at a GC are all things I know from selling to contractors.
screens.why4: Every row is a distinct person with one clear tag, the user and the decider are rightly separate rows since the super doesn't buy, and nothing I didn't name has been added.
screens.why5: The CFO and the project executive appear in the order I typed them, in my words, both tagged as having to agree, with the ops lead as the decider, which is exactly what I said.
screens.why7: The rows follow the card: Nobody else is fixed first, the two named roles are each on one row of at most four words with a plain tag, nothing is added or dropped, and both has-to-agree roles are there for the belief to join with 'and'.

screens.why1: Right after I named the CFO and the project executive as the people who have to agree, Keel asks which version of that belief to test, which is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Every word is plain to me: CFO, project executive, sign off, decides; the only wobble is the placeholder bar saying 'the one you pick' over a single row holding both roles.
screens.why3: Who has to agree before a GC buys a per-site tool is my own sales reality, so I can answer it straight.
screens.why4: The two rows are complete and distinct: the decider alone, or the decider with the two roles I typed, in my words and in my order, with nothing added or dropped.
screens.why5: Both roles I typed are kept as I wrote them, and the belief reads exactly what I meant: the ops lead decides, and the CFO and the project executive must agree first.
screens.why7: The rows follow the card: Nobody else first, then the decider with both named roles joined by 'and', no role Keel invented, and a bar of 2 in 3 counting decided-alone and had-to-agree as for, so the belief can be both supported and refuted; the item naming only the CFO is the card's Open point.
screens.instead: Same screen, with the placeholder bar reading 'or that the CFO and the project executive would have to agree' instead of 'the one you pick', so it matches the single combined row.

screens.why1: Right after naming who decides and who else must agree, asking what my GC customer has to get through before paying is the obvious next step of how it sells.
screens.why2: "What must the buyer's own side clear before they pay" with the hint's example and "not your own trial or pilot" is plain to me on first read; I know exactly what a GC makes a vendor go through.
screens.why3: I sell to general contractors per site, so I know they check it works with Procore or ACC and that IT wants to know where the site videos go.
screens.why4: A free box for up to four steps with a single "I'm not sure" escape is the right shape for my own list, and the escape fits a founder who hasn't sold enough to know.
screens.why5: Both of my steps are kept in my words, a Procore compatibility check and a security review of the site videos, with nothing reworded.
screens.why7: Both rows are brakes on the GC's side that I don't control, each a noun phrase under 9 words with its object, neither is my own trial or pilot, they don't overlap, the larger blocker comes first, and the time is left for me to type next.

screens.why1: Right after I named what my buyer's side has to clear, checking Keel's list of those steps is the obvious next screen before I pick one and type its time.
screens.why2: The rows read plain to me, but the note under the list, 'Keel's draft broke one of its own rules', doesn't say which rule or which row, so I'd stop and reread to work out whether I have to fix something.
screens.why3: Whether a GC's ops lead would check Procore fit, have someone look at where site video is stored, or put new apps on company phones through IT is exactly what I hear on every sales call.
screens.why4: Keel's added IT review of new software on company devices largely overlaps my security review of the site videos, because at most general contractors the same IT person or outside MSP does both in one pass.
screens.why5: My Procore check and my security review of the site videos are kept in my words, and the trial row is gone, which is right since the trial is my own offer.
screens.why7: Both of my rows are real brakes on the buyer's side and Keel added only one row, but that row repeats much of the security review instead of adding a gate this trade has of its own, which bends the no-overlap rule.
screens.instead: Keep 'A check that it works with Procore' and 'A security review of the site videos', and replace Keel's row with one this trade really has, such as 'Sign-off from the project executive on the job', or drop it.

screens.why1: Right after I checked the steps my buyer's side has to clear, it's obvious I now pick one and put my own time on it so the operations leads can be asked about it.
screens.why2: Procore check, security review of the site videos, IT review on company devices: these are the words a GC's ops lead and I use, and 'how long do you expect this step to take' is plain.
screens.why3: I know from selling to GCs that the Procore question comes up first and roughly how long their check takes, so I can answer from my own deals.
screens.why4: Keel's 'IT review of new software on company devices' partly overlaps 'a security review of the site videos', since at most GCs the same IT person signs off both; 'I'm not sure' is the right escape.
screens.why5: My pick, 'a check that it works with Procore', and my 2 weeks appear word for word in the belief and the bar.
screens.why7: All three rows are steps on the buyer's side before paying, none is my own offer; the time is mine (2 weeks), so the edge is my belief; the bar counts under 2 weeks or not needed for, as the card says; and the escape is present.
screens.instead: Keep the screen, but word Keel's row as 'IT approval to put the app on company phones' so it doesn't overlap the security review of the site videos.

screens.why1: After who decides, the cost, the price and the purchase hurdles, asking what first step I'd want the contractor's ops lead to take is the natural last commercial question, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: The step itself is plain to me, but 'and what would it cost them' reads at first as a second question until the hint shows it is one answer, the step with where the money goes, like my 'start a paid pilot on one site'.
screens.why3: I sell per site per month to GCs, so I know exactly what first step I'd ask an ops lead for: a paid pilot on one live job.
screens.why4: It is a free-text box plus the 'I'm not sure' chip, which is right for the founder's side because the card allows that chip to leave the dimension out.
screens.why5: My words 'start a paid pilot on one site' fit the 9-word base-form slot whole, keeping 'paid' and 'one site', with nothing reworded.
screens.why7: The box asks for one step of up to 9 words, says where the money goes, and promises a smaller free step on the next screen only if it costs money, data or a signature; that matches the card's founder `step` shape and its one-step, 'I'm not sure'-allowed registry exactly.
screens.instead: What's the first real step you'd want the contractor operations lead to take, and does it cost them money, data or a signature? (e.g. "pay for a pilot on one job")

screens.why1: Right after I named the paid pilot as my first real step, it makes sense to check how buyers will hear it and the free step before it, as the last commercial check.
screens.why2: The step and the four answers are plain to me, but the smaller-step field reads 'Yes, after a free look at a demo on sample data first' under a label that already says 'a smaller step first', so I have to read it twice to see what I'm keeping.
screens.why3: Whether a GC's operations lead would put one job on a paid pilot, or want to see a demo first, is exactly the call I hear from contractors every week.
screens.why4: The four answers are a firm yes to my pilot, a soft yes after a free demo, probably not, and no: complete, distinct, and in a buyer's words.
screens.why5: My step 'start a paid pilot on one site' is kept whole, but the smaller step lost 'on sample data' between the field and the stranger's option, so what strangers agree to see is not quite what the field says.
screens.why7: The measure, order, balance (two for, two against) and the missing escape all meet the card, but the smaller step is stored as a full answer frame ('Yes, after ... first') instead of a noun phrase, and the served option trims it, so one shape rule is bent.
screens.instead: Smaller step: 'a free demo on sample data'; options: Yes, I'd start a paid pilot on one site · Probably, after a free demo on sample data first · Probably not · No.

screens.why1: Right after I set the commitment step and just before strangers see the study, it makes sense to ask whether to collect real names for that step.
screens.why2: 'Offer a pilot?' is plain to me, and the hint spells out exactly what the respondent sees and where I find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want pilot sign-ups is my own call, and I know I do because a paid pilot on one site is my first step.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it cleanly, and no escape is needed for a founder's own choice.
screens.why5: My step was 'start a paid pilot on one site', but the line respondents get, 'Would you try this for real?', drops the paid part and the per-site part, so a super could say yes to a free try I'm not offering.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes get a line at the end: "Would you start a paid pilot of this on one of your sites? Leave your email." (Yes, ask them / No pilot)

screens.why1: Saving the study and settling who asks the questions on the AI link is the natural last step before strangers see it, right after the pilot offer.
screens.why2: "Save your answers" is plain, but "lock and record the face Keel preselects" makes me stop: I'm not sure if "face" means the AI interviewer, or what "lock" and "record" commit me to.
screens.why3: It's my study and my call whether to keep Keel's default interviewer, so I can answer it from what I know.
screens.why4: Accepting the preselected face is a fair default, but from the label alone I can't tell how it differs from choosing another, or whether I can change it later.
screens.why5: Nothing I typed about Fresco, superintendents or the contractor buyer is reworded here, so my words are kept.
screens.instead: Save your study: Keel picked the AI interviewer who will ask your questions on the call (keep this one / pick another), and you can change it before you send the link.

screens.why1: Choosing how strangers take the study is the natural last step after saving my answers and before I send the link.
screens.why2: The options are clear, but the bare question "New link" doesn't say what I'm choosing (how people will answer), so I read the options to work it out.
screens.why3: I know my supers and ops leads: on phones, often in a trailer or a truck, so I can judge which format they would actually do.
screens.why4: Three distinct, complete formats with plain descriptions and a sensible "let them choose"; nothing missing.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles is changed or leaked; the screen is only about delivery format.
screens.instead: How should people answer this link? -- Read and tap / A video interviewer asks aloud / Let them pick

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits under the title with its deciding number beside it (Price: 1 of 8 at $800 or more per site a month), so I know the money side fails and that price is the reason.
screens.why_b2: Each card's count and bar are plain (e.g. 5 of 8 against a bar of 6 of 8, 1 short), but the kicker's '1 TO 8 COUNTED' and the split between 'not holding' and 'did not hold' in the tally need a second look.
screens.why_b3: These are my six beliefs in my own words: 30 to 60 hours a month on the log, $800 to $1,000 per site, the operations lead deciding with the CFO and project executive, the Procore check within 2 weeks, and a paid pilot on one site.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do next, such as whether to drop toward the $100-$300 range, reprice against the 40 hours the leads say they lose, or offer a free pilot instead of a paid one; 'What it measures' only explains the method.
screens.why_b5: The n stays visible and the too-few card is called, but the banner says every answer is the operations lead's while card 1 states supers' hours as holding without saying these are the leads' estimates, and the headline says 'Not holding up' while two cards say the stronger 'did not hold', despite 'the worst of all its cards' rule.
screens.instead: Not holding: only 1 of 8 contractor ops leads would pay $800+ a site a month, though 5 of 7 say their supers lose 30+ hours a month on logs; and only 3 of 8 would start a paid pilot. Next, test a lower price or a free one-site pilot priced against those hours.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "5 of 7 spend 30 hours or more per site a month · bar 5 of 7 · at the bar", so I know the belief held and by what count, just barely.
screens.why_b2: The strip says it counts hours of the daily log per site a month, one cell per person over 7 counted, with my bar marked at 5 of 7 (at least 2 in 3) and the median at 40 hours.
screens.why_b3: It's my 30 to 60 hours per site a month on the daily log, but my group was "construction superintendents on commercial jobs" and the card drops "on commercial jobs".
screens.why_b4: "The cost is there" plus a pointer to the Price card is a handoff, not a next step: it doesn't say that a 40-hour median is worth well over my $800 price, and the price still failed on the stage page.
screens.why_b5: The small group is flagged ("a lean, not a call") and Faith's none-as-0 is explained, but Trevor's "10.9 hours" looks like a dollar amount converted at some rate the screen never mentions, shown as if he'd said hours.
screens.instead: Holding up, just: 5 of 7 contractors put 30+ hours per site a month on the daily log (median 40, about $2,200 at $55 an hour, above your $800 price), but the price still fails, so sell the hours saved, not the software; Trevor's 10.9 hours is his part-time document controller's pay turned into hours.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits right beside its deciding number, 1 of 8 at $800 or more against a bar of 6 of 8, so I know at once that my price failed.
screens.why_b2: Each band shows its count and whether it is for or against, the strip shows 1 for and 7 against out of 8, and the marker at 6 shows where the bar is, all on first look.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Price and the belief is the one I checked: contractor operations leads would think Fresco worth $800 to $1,000 per site a month.
screens.why_b4: The So line says where people landed (5 of 8 under $500) and sends me to another tab, but it doesn't say what to do: the quotes point to a free one-job pilot, per-user pricing, or showing the hours first, and the screen leaves me to work that out.
screens.why_b5: The n of 8 stays visible, the screen says plainly that this is 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and it claims nothing beyond the eight who answered.
screens.instead: Only 1 of 8 would pay $800, and most put Fresco under $500 a site, though you measured about 40 hours a month going into logs; they don't count those hours as money they spend, so show the hours or start with a free one-job pilot before you defend $1k.

screens.why_b1: 'Too few to call' sits right beside '1 of 8 named your price or more · 5 needed', so I know nothing is decided and exactly why.
screens.why_b2: The bars plainly count where Gordon's money would come from, but the strip's 'your bar · 4 of 5 (at least 2 in 3)' with four ghost cells next to '1 answered' takes a second look to see it means 4 of the 5 I'd need, not 4 of 5 I have.
screens.why_b3: My buyer and my $800 to $1,000 per site a month are there, but I never typed or checked an ability-to-pay belief; Keel derived it, and the card calls it 'Your belief' as though I had.
screens.why_b4: 'Ability to pay waits until 5 have' tells me to wait, but not that this is blocked by Price: only Gordon reached $800, so the move is to fix price or buyer, not to collect more answers.
screens.why_b5: 'a lean, not a call' still reads one person as a lean, and the rule line leaves out 'Charged back to whoever uses it' (for) and 'New money from outside' (against) while naming a 'none' the list doesn't offer.
screens.instead: Too few to call: only Gordon of 8 reached $800, and his money would need a new budget line; this waits on Price, so settle the price or who you're selling to before asking where the money comes from.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 8 as you said or easier · bar 6 of 8 · at the bar', so I know it held and by what number, if only just.
screens.why_b2: Four bars in order with for/against tags, 8 people, and the strip's marker at 6 of 8 under 'at least 2 in 3' make what is counted, over whom, and where the bar sits plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: The card's name and belief line are mine: the operations lead decides and the CFO and the project executive agree; the bar line narrows that to the CFO, but the belief is as I set it.
screens.why_b4: 'Plan for the CFO in most deals; 2 of 8 could sign alone' tells me concretely to build the CFO into my sales motion, though it says nothing about the project executive I also named.
screens.why_b5: 'A lean, not a call' keeps the small n honest, but 'as you said' and 'in most deals' stretch it: only 4 of 8 named the CFO, which is half, not most, and nobody was asked about the project executive, so the half of my belief that names them was never tested.
screens.instead: Holding up, just at the bar: 6 of 8 could sign alone or with the CFO; 4 of 8 need the CFO, so plan for the CFO in half your deals; the project executive was not asked about, so test that separately.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside 5 of 8 against a bar of 6 of 8, one short, so I know the result and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The bands, the for/against tags, the 8 people and the marker at 6 are plain, and the note that my 2 weeks is the low edge of the against band explains why 2 weeks to 1 month counts against me.
screens.why_b3: The Procore check is a step from my own list, but the 2 weeks I typed was for the trial on one live job, which Keel dropped, so the time is now attached to a step I didn't pick it for.
screens.why_b4: It tells me to plan for a 2-weeks-to-1-month Procore check rather than my 2 weeks, and where to look for what eats the time.
screens.why_b5: The count line says this is a lean on 8 people and not a call, yet the status says a flat "Did not hold" and the So line tells me to plan the cycle around 3 people, which is a little firmer than the data carries.
screens.instead: Leaning against, on 8: 3 of 8 operations leads, one more than your bar allows, think a Procore check would take 2 weeks to 1 month, not your 2 weeks; budget up to a month for it and see Insights for what slows it.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Did not hold' sits right beside '3 of 8 said yes · bar 6 of 8 · 3 short', and the numbers agree with the rule of no more than 1 in 3 against.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over all 8 operations leads, 3 for and 5 against, and the strip marks my bar at 6, all plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: Commitment is the dimension I set, and 'start a paid pilot on one site' with the operations lead deciding is my step and my decider, though the rule line's 'a free look at a demo on sample data' does not quite match the chart's 'a free look at a demo'.
screens.why_b4: The So line only repeats the 5 and sends me to the Insights tab; it doesn't say that nobody took the free demo route either, so the five are a real no to paying, not a call for a cheaper first step.
screens.why_b5: The count line says 'a lean, not a call' over 8, which is right, but the So line turns three 'probably not' answers into '5 of 8 would not', which firms up a soft no.

screens.why_b1: Each box states its verdict word with the deciding count beside it: Price 1 of 8 against a bar of 6, Purchase friction 5 of 8 and 1 short, Commitment 3 of 8 and 3 short; only the mixed wording 'Not holding up' versus 'Did not hold' jars a little.
screens.why_b3: Price, Purchase friction and Commitment are my names, and the belief lines (the $800 to $1,000 per site a month, the Procore check within about 2 weeks, the paid pilot on one site) are the ones I checked.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what to do. The quotes point at moves: show buyers the hours first, offer a free month on one job, price per active super. Purchase friction and Commitment, two failed lines, carry no reasons at all, and the screen doesn't say that's a gap to close.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible throughout. But 'never saw it (Bill, Gordon)' and '1 asked on Price' / '2 asked on Price' leave me unsure how someone who never saw a line is counted against it, and which Price quotes belong to Commitment or Purchase friction (Renee's free-month answer is plainly a Commitment answer filed under Price).
screens.why_b6: These are things I did not type. Buyers can't see the hours, so they won't fund it. Overtime caps what they'd pay at about $600. They want a free month before any paid pilot and per-user rather than per-site pricing. Some won't trust an app with the legal record of a dispute, and a second fee on top of Procore is hard to justify.
screens.instead: Price fails at 1 of 8: three buyers can't see what logs cost them, so show them the hours; Renee and Lena point to a free first month and per-user pricing, which also explains why Commitment fails. Purchase friction and Commitment have no reasons of their own yet, so ask those 8 why next.

screens.why1: This is the idea I'm being asked to judge as the person who would buy it, so reading it first on the buying-decision link makes sense, even with no warm-up before it.
screens.why2: Site walks, short videos, assignees, due dates, Procore and ACC are all words I use every week, and 'AI scribe' is clear enough from the line after it.
screens.why3: I know how my supers walk the site and how the daily log and punch items get into Procore, so I can picture this on my own jobs.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks that shouldn't, but the last line, 'would give you all of that', tells me nothing the builders actually believe, such as time saved or a better log, so their claim has thinned to an echo.
screens.why6: Short plain sentences with no parentheses or slashes; 'ACC' said as letters is how we say it anyway, and only the last line sounds hollow out loud.
screens.instead: Keep the first two paragraphs, and end with what they think it does for me, e.g. 'The people building it believe your supers' daily logs would be done and in Procore before they leave site.'

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, asking what the daily log already costs us per site is the obvious first question about the buying decision, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: Daily log, hours per site and last month are how I talk about it; I'd read it once and know what's wanted.
screens.why3: I pay for the supers' time but nobody tracks daily-log hours on their own, so my answer would be an estimate from what the supers tell me, not a figure I know.
screens.why4: A box for the hours, None, and I can't recall cover every answer I'd give, and the one escape fits.
screens.why5: It is the founder's own measure, hours per site a month on the daily log, and nothing of the product or its roles shows through.
screens.why6: It is one short question with a plain unit and one escape, easy to answer after hearing it once, though 'A number of hours per site last month' is a little redundant.
screens.why7: The box uses the founder's unit, base and period (hours per site a month on the daily log), so any answer can be placed above or below the founder's 30, and the one required escape is there.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the hours question, asking what it's worth to me per site is exactly where price belongs, and I'm the one who pays.
screens.why2: Per site, per month is how we buy software for our jobs, and the dollar bands are plain.
screens.why3: I pay for tools by the job site every month, so I can answer this from what I already spend.
screens.why4: The bands don't overlap, they cover the whole range, wouldn't pay is there, and I can't say sits apart as the one escape.
screens.why5: Only the named idea card reaches me; nothing of the founder's plan or their words for people leaks into the question.
screens.why6: Short stem, four options said once, the escape last, then a two-option follow-up; I can hold that on a call.
screens.why7: One measure in the founder's per-site monthly unit, six rungs with an edge exactly at $800, two bands plus wouldn't pay against and three for, and the escape is I can't say alone.

screens.why1: Right after I put a number on it, asking what would push that number up is the obvious next question for the person who pays.
screens.why2: It plays my pick back the way I'd say it, about $500 to $800 a site a month, and asks a plain question I can answer in a sentence.
screens.why3: I know what my sites spend on the daily log and what I'd need to see before paying more, like Procore sync or less super time.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: Fresco is the name from the idea card I was shown, and nothing else of the founder's plan or terms comes through.
screens.why6: Said aloud it is one short playback and one question, and the dollar range says cleanly.

screens.why1: Right after I named what Fresco would be worth to me a site a month, asking whether I can sign that off myself or need the CFO is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: Sign off, CFO and per site a month are how we talk about software spend at a GC, so I can answer it on first read.
screens.why3: Choosing and paying for job-site software is my job, so I know exactly where my approval limit sits and when the CFO has to see it.
screens.why4: The four run cleanly from me alone to the CFO to a group to not my call, each one distinct, and I can't say fits as the way out.
screens.why5: The CFO is a role every GC I know has, the price is the one I just gave, and nothing of the product's pitch or the founder's own terms comes through.
screens.why6: It is one short either-or question, four short options said as a list I can hold, and one escape at the end; Or say: I can't say is a little stiff but clear.
screens.why7: Every option is on who has to agree, the four are in order from alone to someone else's call with the CFO named in the second, the first two can support the founder and the last two refute, and I can't say is there apart.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I or the CFO signs off, asking what else stands between wanting it and buying it is the obvious next thing for someone like me who picks and pays for the software.
screens.why2: A check that it works with Procore is exactly how I'd say it, since every new tool on our jobs gets that question first.
screens.why3: I'm the one who runs or chases that check, so I know roughly how long it takes us, depending on whether the tool's already in the Procore marketplace or needs our IT to look at it.
screens.why4: The bands cover the range I'd expect, from a few days to a quarter, plus it wouldn't be needed if it's already a listed Procore app, and I can't tell fits a tool I haven't bought.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's pitch or their words for people reaches me here; it's just Fresco and a check against the system we already run.
screens.why6: Said aloud, it's one short question, four options I can hold (under 2 weeks, 2 weeks to 1 month, over 1 month, not needed), then a two-way follow-up, with nothing that only reads on the page.
screens.why7: Every option is one measure, how long the buyer-side Procore check takes; the band edge sits at 2 weeks, so under 1 week, 1 to under 2 weeks and not needed count for and 2 weeks to 1 month and longer count against; the escape is the one I can't tell.

screens.why1: After price, sign-off and the Procore check, asking whether I'd actually start a pilot is the obvious last buying question for the person who picks and pays for site software.
screens.why2: A paid pilot on one site is exactly how I'd trial a tool across our jobs, so I can answer it on first read.
screens.why3: I'm the one who would approve a pilot on a job site, so this is my own call to make.
screens.why4: Firm yes, soft yes after a demo, probably not and no are distinct, cover how I'd really answer, and the demo is a believable free step before paying.
screens.why5: The paid pilot on one site comes through as a plain offer in my words, and nothing of the founder's own terms leaks beyond the idea card shown on purpose.
screens.why6: One short question and four short options read as a list I can hold after hearing it once.
